title: Psalm 131: Like a Weaned Child
summary: In three short verses the psalmist tells the LORD that his heart is not proud and his eyes not haughty, and that he does not reach for things too great for him. He has calmed and quieted his soul, like a weaned child resting with its mother. Then he turns to the whole people: Israel, hope in the LORD, now and forever.
story: Psalm 130 cried from the depths and waited through the night for the LORD. Psalm 131 is what the waiting soul looks like when it has become still. Both psalms end with the same call, “O Israel, put your hope in the LORD”, and the pairing seems deliberate: after the confession of sin and the promise of redemption comes the quiet of a person who has stopped demanding. It is one of the shortest psalms in the Bible. In the sequence of the Songs of Ascents it comes just before Psalm 132, the longest of the collection, which turns from the humility of one soul to the great promises God made to David.
historical:
The heading reads “A song of ascents. Of David.” As elsewhere, the Hebrew phrase can mean by, for, or about David, and the attribution is not found in every ancient manuscript. Readers who connect the psalm with David point to his humility in accepting God's timing: he refused to seize the throne from Saul even when he had the chance (1 Samuel 24 and 26), and when he was forced out of Jerusalem during Absalom's revolt he left his return in God's hands (2 Samuel 15:25-26). His dancing before the ark, when he said he would become even more undignified (2 Samuel 6:21-22), is sometimes connected too. Others read the psalm as the prayer of an unnamed worshiper, perhaps after the exile, since the final verse addresses the whole community. The psalm gives no historical details, and its value does not depend on the setting.

A few interpreters have suggested, from the image of the mother and child, that the psalm may have been written by a woman. The text does not say, and the question remains open; what is clear is that the psalm uses a mother's care as a picture of the soul's rest in God.
cultural:
In ancient Israel children were usually nursed much longer than is common in the modern West, often until about two or three years old. Weaning was a milestone: Abraham held a great feast on the day Isaac was weaned (Genesis 21:8), and Hannah waited until Samuel was weaned before bringing him to serve at the sanctuary at Shiloh (1 Samuel 1:22-24). A nursing infant cries and reaches for the breast whenever it is hungry. A weaned child has learned to be with its mother without demanding to be fed, content simply to be near her. That is the picture of the soul in verse 2: no longer restless and grasping, but quiet in the presence of the one who cares for it.

The language of verse 1 also draws on common Hebrew idioms. A lifted heart and raised eyes described pride and ambition, the posture of someone who looks down on others or reaches above his place. Things too wonderful (the Hebrew word often describes God's marvelous deeds) are matters beyond human grasp. The psalmist does not claim to understand everything; he has made peace with not needing to.
literary: Psalm 131 is a psalm of trust in three verses. The first uses three negatives (not proud, not haughty, not reaching for great things) to clear away pride. The second makes a strong positive statement, beginning with a Hebrew oath formula (literally, surely I have), and repeats the image of the weaned child in a stair-step pattern: “like a weaned child with his mother, like a weaned child is my soul within me.” The third turns from the individual to the nation, with the same call that ends Psalm 130. The movement is from what the psalmist refuses, to what he has done, to what he invites others to do. Its brevity is part of its meaning: a quiet soul does not need many words.

outline.t: Not proud, not reaching for things too great
A quieted soul, like a weaned child with its mother
Israel, hope in the LORD forever

doctrines.note: Faith here is not a set of answers but a posture: stillness and trust in the presence of God, without demanding that he explain everything or give everything at once.
The psalm ends with a call to hope in the LORD “both now and forevermore.” Hope is linked to humility; it is the quiet confidence of someone who does not need to control the future.
The psalm accepts the limits of being human. There are matters too great and too wonderful for us, and acknowledging that is not failure but wisdom.

words.note: Gamal, to wean, to deal fully with, to complete. The word can describe finishing something or dealing with someone, but its most vivid use is for weaning a child. The image of the weaned child with its mother is the psalm's center, and it appears twice in verse 2.

Damam, to be silent, still, or quiet. It describes the stillness of someone who has stopped protesting or striving. Psalm 62:1 uses a related word for the soul waiting in silence for God. Here the psalmist has actively stilled his own soul, as a mother calms a child.

Pala, to be wonderful or extraordinary. It usually describes God's marvelous deeds, things beyond human power or understanding. The psalmist declines to occupy himself with things too wonderful for him, recognizing that some matters belong to God alone.

christ: The New Testament does not quote Psalm 131, but Jesus teaches its heart. He says that unless people turn and become like children they will not enter the kingdom of heaven, and that whoever humbles himself like a child is greatest in it (Matthew 18:3-4). He describes himself as gentle and lowly in heart and promises rest to those who come to him (Matthew 11:28-29). Paul describes Christ as one who did not grasp at equality with God but humbled himself, taking the form of a servant, and he urges believers to have the same mind (Philippians 2:5-8). In the garden before his death, Jesus prayed not my will but yours (Luke 22:42), the ultimate stilling of the soul before the Father. The link is thematic: the humility of the psalm is embodied in the one who humbled himself for others.
questions: What are the things too great or too wonderful for you that you keep trying to understand or control?
The weaned child is content to be near its mother without demanding. What would it look like for you to be with God without asking for something?
The psalmist says he has stilled and quieted his own soul. What practices help you do that?
